title: India Maps Semiconductor Roadmap From 28nm to 3nm as Chip Design Push Accelerates
excerpt: India targets 2-3nm chip production by 2032, with Renesas design center in Noida marking the country's first 3nm chip design facility and IIT Madras developing an indigenous 7nm processor.
body:
• India has mapped a semiconductor roadmap from 28nm to 7nm to 3nm to 2nm, targeting 2-3nm chip production by 2032 and 2nm by 2035.
  • Renesas Electronics inaugurated India's first 3nm chip design center in Noida, while IIT Madras is developing the indigenous 7nm 'Shakti' processor for completion by 2028.
  • Under the India Semiconductor Mission, 24 chip design firms have been selected and startups have attracted nearly ₹430 crore in venture capital funding.
  • The ISM 2.0 program includes a $4.8 billion equipment and materials budget, with 10 fab projects under construction and four expected to begin production this year.

A Phased Approach to Chip Sovereignty

India's semiconductor ambitions are taking concrete shape as the government charts a technology roadmap from mature 28-nanometer nodes to cutting-edge 3nm and 2nm chip fabrication, a journey that IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw has described as a carefully studied path modeled on the semiconductor trajectories of Taiwan, Japan, and South Korea.

"We have mapped out the path from 28nm to 7nm to 3nm to 2nm," Vaishnaw said earlier this year. "With these six systems, we can manufacture 70-75 per cent of all the major defence, consumer electronics, industrial electronics and the critical other applications we need."

The plan centers on six chip categories under the second phase of the Design Linked Incentive (DLI) scheme: compute, radio frequency, networking, power, sensor, and memory. The government aims for Indian companies to control the development of 70-75 percent of technology product types in these areas.

3nm Design Marks a New Frontier

In a milestone for India's chip design capabilities, Renesas Electronics inaugurated two state-of-the-art design facilities in Noida and Bengaluru, with the Noida center becoming India's first facility to work on 3nm chip design. Vaishnaw called it a "new frontier," noting that while Indian engineers have previously designed 7nm and 5nm chips at domestic facilities, the 3nm capability places India in a rarefied global league.

"Designing at 3nm is truly next-generation. We've done 7nm and 5nm earlier, but this marks a new frontier."

— Ashwini Vaishnaw, Union Minister for Electronics and IT

Separately, a team at IIT Madras is developing 'Shakti,' India's first indigenously designed 7nm computer processor targeted at IT servers for financial, communications, defense, and strategic sectors. The chip design is expected to be ready by 2028, coinciding with the timeline for India's wafer fabrication capacity to come online.

ISM 2.0: From Design to Fabrication

The India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 introduces a rigorous technical roadmap, shifting focus from 28nm-to-90nm mature nodes toward the goal of domestic 3nm pilot production by 2032 and full-scale 2nm manufacturing by 2035. The transition requires moving from Deep Ultraviolet (DUV) lithography systems to Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) lithography, a leap that ISM 2.0 supports with a specialized equipment and materials sub-scheme budgeted at approximately $4.8 billion.

On the fabrication front, the Tata group has pledged ₹91,000 crore to build India's first 28nm wafer fab, while Micron Technology's assembly and test facility has begun producing the first "Made in India" chips for the global market. Across 10 approved projects involving $18 billion in investment, four are expected to begin production this year.

Building the Talent Pipeline

The DLI scheme has selected 24 chip design firms under the Semicon India program, many of which have already completed tape-outs, validated products, and gained market traction. Among them, 14 startups have secured venture capital funding totaling nearly ₹430 crore, reflecting growing investor confidence in India's semiconductor ecosystem.

India has also trained 67,000 students in semiconductor chip design across 315 academic institutions, with access to advanced Electronic Design Automation (EDA) tools. Students are designing chips, taping them out at the Semiconductor Laboratory in Mohali, and validating final products, a capability that Vaishnaw has described as rare among countries worldwide.

The Challenge Ahead

The gap with global leaders remains significant. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company is already producing 3nm chips, with 2nm expected in the near term. India's current manufacturing capability starts at 28nm, and the leap to leading-edge nodes requires not just equipment but also deep expertise in Gate-All-Around transistor architectures that will replace current FinFET designs.

Industry observers note that India's chip design strength, with engineering teams at Qualcomm, ARM, NXP, and Renesas designing advanced chips from Indian facilities, remains distinct from chip fabrication sovereignty. The intellectual property for most designs created in India is still owned by foreign parent companies.

Still, the pace of investment and policy commitment has shifted the conversation. "By 2035, the entire world now believes that India will be among the most important nations globally," Vaishnaw said, projecting confidence in a semiconductor strategy that has moved from paper to concrete within three years.
